o: Remove edges so at most k connected components remain, minimizing the maximum component cost (max edge weight inside a component; 0 for isolated vertices). Removing edges never merges components, so if a threshold X lets us keep only edges of weight <= X and yields c(X) components, c is non-increasing in X. Hence binary search the smallest threshold X whose spanning subgraph has at most k components; the answer is that X (or 0 if the graph already has <= k components with no edges kept).
k: Keeping exactly the edges with weight <= X minimizes component cost for that threshold; fewer kept edges only helps.
Component count is monotone non-increasing in X, enabling binary search over sorted distinct weights.
DSU gives the component count for a candidate threshold in near-linear time.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search on threshold + DSU
a.i: Sort distinct edge weights, binary search the smallest X such that the subgraph of edges with weight <= X has <= k components. Monotonicity holds because adding heavier edges can only merge components.
s: Collect and sort distinct weights; prepend sentinel 0.
feasible(X): activate DSU unions for edges with w <= X and count roots.
Binary search the smallest feasible X; return it.
a.t: O(E alpha(n) log E) — binary search over distinct weights, each check a DSU pass.
a.sp: O(N + E) for DSU and the candidate list.

w: Equivalent view: this is like Kruskal stopped early — the answer is the weight of the (m - (k-1))-th smallest edge in a maximum spanning forest sense. Pitfall: remembering 0 as a candidate (when n <= k you can delete everything), and that the input graph is connected so a full-spanning threshold always exists. Follow-up: parallelize with a Kruskal-style sweep computing component counts for all thresholds in one pass.
